steps.prompt: Which one makes you feel like you're there?
steps.a: The fair was busy. There were lots of rides and people.
steps.b: The fair smelled of hot sugar and diesel. Music thumped from the dodgems, and my shoes stuck to the spilled lemonade.
steps.reveal: The first one only tells you what's there. The second uses smell, sound and touch, so you can almost stand in it. That's sensory detail.

cards.title: Sensory detail
cards.body: Sensory details are words that show what you can see, hear, smell, taste and touch. Most writers lean on sight. When you add the other four, readers stop reading about a place and start feeling they're in it.

cards.title: One moment, five senses
cards.text: The bonfire crackled (sound). Orange sparks spiralled into the dark (sight). Smoke stung my eyes and clung to my jumper (smell, touch), and the toasted marshmallow burned my tongue (taste).
cards.note: You don't need all five in every sentence. Spread them through your scene.

cards.title: Name it, or sense it?
cards.showing: The kitchen smelled of warm cinnamon and burnt toast.
cards.note: “Nice” could mean anything. Specific smells let the reader smell it too.

cards.title: Find the senses
cards.prompt: Tap the two words that use senses other than sight.
cards.text: The old library was dim and dusty, and the floorboards creaked while the musty pages crumbled under my fingers.

prompts: Which sense was easiest to write about? Which was hardest?
Which word from your word bank did you use, and why that one?
